raw_record.support_text: Based on the course of laboratory parameters over time, normal ultrasound findings, and the absence of other hepatotoxic agents, the authors conclude that the patient developed hepatic/cholestatic hepatitis as a result of temozolomide (TMZ) treatment. Although histological confirmation was declined, the hepatitis was detected early (normal bilirubin at detection), TMZ was discontinued early, and the patient survived the toxicity, in contrast to the fatal liver failure case reported by the German Drug Commission.
raw_record.extra_details: TMZ is an alkylating cytostatic drug, orally administered, converted to active metabolite MTIC; undergoes renal elimination; frequently reported hepatic side effects include elevation of AST, ALT and GGT. Only a few cases of severe liver damage due to TMZ have been reported; most were associated with hepatitis virus reactivation or interaction with other hepatotoxic drugs, while Goldbecker and Dixit described individual cases of hepatotoxicity caused by TMZ alone. In the reported patient, serum bilirubin and liver enzymes normalized during follow-up but GGT remained elevated; jaundice resolved and no neurological symptoms developed over 3 months; patient had glioblastoma and was lost to further follow-up after the third month. The German Drug Commission (2011) reported a fatal case of liver failure concurrent with leukocytopenia in which bilirubin reached 11 mg/dl and rose more than twofold, ending in death from hepatic encephalopathy and liver failure. Literature cases: bilirubin 11 mg/dl, MTIC, Goldbecker case, German Drug Commission case, TMZ monotherapy.

raw_record.extra_details: Eight cases of propafenone hepatotoxicity presented (2 new patients plus 7 previously reported). Presents as cholestatic hepatitis with jaundice in most; latency 2-6 weeks except one case at 28 weeks; injury resolved progressively after drug discontinuation. ALT ranged 22-501 IU/L, ALP up to 1512 IU/L, gamma-GT up to 890 IU/L; eosinophilia (2-11%) in most cases suggested a hypersensitivity reaction as the pathogenic mechanism, though neither of the paper's two patients had eosinophilia. One patient had transient ANA positivity. Liver biopsies showed portal tract enlargement with mononuclear infiltrates, bile duct proliferation with injury, ballooning of hepatocytes, and cholestasis with biliary thrombi. Clinical abnormalities improved after propafenone discontinuation even while the patient continued digitoxin and enalapril, supporting propafenone as the cause. Authors note relatively low frequency, making routine ALT monitoring unnecessary, but abdominal symptoms or jaundice should prompt hepatotoxicity consideration.

Case 2 was diagnosed with loratidine-induced hepatitis, confirmed by rechallenge (resuming loratidine 10 mg daily promptly raised ALT to 1,800 U/L, AST to 1,027 U/L, bilirubin to 3.9 mg/dL), resolving after rechallenge discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: Two cases at 10 mg daily oral therapeutic dosing. Case 1 (49y male): ALT 675 U/L, AST 305 U/L, bilirubin 2.9 mg/dL, INR 1.2, biopsy showed panacinar/portal hepatitis with lymphocytic infiltrate sparing bile ducts, grade 4/4 hepatitis with zone necrosis but no fibrosis; positive antismooth muscle antibody (1:40) and circulating immune complexes; both recovered after loratidine discontinuation (normal biochemistries for 10 years). Case 2 (50y male): jaundice/fatigue, bilirubin 9.1 mg/dL, ALT 2,495 U/L, ALP 189 U/L; biopsy showed chronic hepatitis with lymphocytic infiltrate, eosinophils, plasma cells and portal fibrosis; positive anti-F1 actin (1:31) and anti-mitochondrial antibody (1:88); rechallenge confirmed causality; treated with prednisone and ursodeoxycholic acid, normal biochemistries for 1.5 years. Authors suggest loratidine triggered immune-mediated injury resembling overlap between autoimmune hepatitis and primary biliary cirrhosis; no other medications, alcohol, or herbs taken.

raw_record.support_text: Propofol is commonly used as an anesthetic agent for invasive procedures. The paper reports a case of idiosyncratic drug induced liver injury (DILI) in a 39-year-old female after a brief exposure to propofol during routine endoscopy. Within 48 hours of discharge she was hospitalized with abdominal pain, nausea, and laboratory abnormalities consistent with hepatocellular injury; serologic workup for viral and autoimmune etiologies was negative, and the transaminase abnormalities improved by hospital day three and resolved by two week follow up. The RUCAM score was highly suggestive of an adverse drug reaction, and this was described as only the fourth case report of propofol-related DILI.

raw_record.support_text: A 41-year-old female presented with a skin rash and abnormal liver function tests after the recent initiation of fluoxetine. Skin and liver biopsies showed features of Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and drug-induced liver injury (DILI), respectively. Fluoxetine was stopped, after which her liver function tests and skin rash improved without progression to fulminant hepatic failure. The authors present this as the first described case of fluoxetine-induced SJS and DILI, noting that fluoxetine is associated with an asymptomatic increase in liver enzymes in 0.5% of cases and that only a handful of prior case reports describe isolated fluoxetine-induced DILI presenting as an acute hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: First described case of concomitant DILI and SJS secondary to fluoxetine in a 41-year-old female. Skin and liver biopsies showed features of SJS and DILI, respectively. Fluoxetine was discontinued with subsequent improvement in liver function tests and skin rash, without progression to fulminant hepatic failure. Fluoxetine is associated with an asymptomatic increase in liver enzymes in 0.5% of cases, but is rarely associated with FHF or SJS; a handful of prior case reports describe isolated fluoxetine-induced DILI presenting as an acute hepatitis. DILI is described as an idiosyncratic, dose-independent reaction dependent on age, sex, and genetic polymorphisms of drug-metabolizing enzymes such as cytochrome P450.

raw_record.support_text: The authors attribute prolonged cholestasis in their patient to amitriptyline based on: absence of biliary tract disease (normal retrograde cholangiography and ultrasound), no serologic or circumstantial evidence of viral hepatitis, negative serum antitissue antibodies, and discontinuation of other drugs 2 weeks before jaundice onset without reported hepatotoxicity. The clinical presentation (jaundice after 5 weeks of amitriptyline, transient eosinophilia, initial centrilobular cholestasis) resembled previously reported amitriptyline-induced acute cholestatic hepatitis. Despite stopping amitriptyline, cholestasis was markedly protracted, with pruritus and jaundice lasting 19 and 20 months and abnormal liver tests persisting at 2 years; three liver biopsies showed progression from centrilobular cholestasis to portal inflammation, ductular proliferation, moderate fibrosis, and partial disappearance of interlobular bile ducts.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient case report. Jaundice onset 5 weeks after starting amitriptyline, accompanied by transient blood eosinophilia. Three serial liver biopsies documented initial centrilobular cholestasis progressing to portal inflammatory infiltration, ductular proliferation, moderate fibrosis, and partial loss of interlobular bile ducts. Competing causes excluded (no biliary disease, no viral hepatitis, negative antitissue antibodies). Hepatitis suggested to be immunoallergic; a reactive-metabolite/immune mechanism analogous to imipramine/amineptine was hypothesized. Debrisoquine/dextromethorphan oxidation phenotyping showed an extensive metabolizer phenotype (metabolic ratio 0.009), indicating amitriptyline hydroxylation was not deficient.

raw_record.support_text: In a case series of 30 patients with metformin-induced hepatotoxicity, metformin was discontinued in all patients. Four patients (13.3%) were rechallenged with metformin and two of them relapsed with hepatotoxicity. Liver function returned to normal in all 30 patients (100%) at a median time of 6 weeks (range 2–16), while two patients had persistently high ALP levels.

Biopsy (13 patients) showed portal inflammation (61.5%), cholestatic hepatitis (38.5%), parenchymal inflammation (38.5%), bile duct inflammation with epithelial destruction (23.1%), fibrosis (15.4%). raw_record.support_text: The clinical picture observed in 1979 and 1981 after propafenone treatment (Propafenon) is described as speaking for a drug-induced cholestatic hepatitis. A drug-allergic hepatitis was considered compatible with the liver enzyme patterns; other potentially hepatotoxic drugs, alcohol, extrahepatic obstruction, and viral hepatitis were excluded. Lymphocyte stimulation tests performed 2 weeks later using therapeutically effective propafenone serum concentrations showed a clear proliferation rate, which the authors state confirms this diagnosis.

In-vitro lymphocyte stimulation (metabolite serum or propafenone) of patient lymphocytes yielded 3.6-fold and 2.9-fold proliferation rates versus a control person, supporting the drug-allergic diagnosis. Propafenone has high affinity for lung and liver tissue. The reaction is rare but should be considered in differential diagnosis of unclear cholestasis.

raw_record.support_text: A case report attributes cholestatic jaundice, rash, and eosinophilia to aminoglutethimide, appearing after several weeks of sensitization, as a systemic hypersensitivity reaction. The authors state there was no evidence of infectious hepatitis or another hepatotoxin administration, and propose an idiosyncratic hypersensitivity mechanism similar to phenytoin and sulfa compounds, possibly indicating a latent direct hepatotoxic potential of aminoglutethimide.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient presented with rash, eosinophilia, and cholestatic jaundice after several weeks of sensitization, suggesting an idiosyncratic hypersensitivity reaction similar to that seen with phenytoin and sulfa compounds; the case was not rechallenged with aminoglutethimide and no liver biopsy was performed. The authors consider a toxic effect of the androgenic precursors androstenedione and testosterone (increased via aromatase inhibition) less likely, noting these compounds lack the 17-alkyl group thought needed for hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Although the patient was not rechallenged with aminoglutethimide and did not undergo liver biopsy, the authors concluded the case likely represents a systemic hypersensitivity reaction to aminoglutethimide causing cholestatic jaundice after several weeks of sensitization. The presence of rash and eosinophilia along with the cholestatic jaundice suggested an idiosyncratic hypersensitivity mechanism, similar to phenytoin and sulfa compounds, with a less likely contributing role considered for the aromatase-inhibited androgenic precursors androstenedione and testosterone. The patient's icterus and liver tests resolved after aminoglutethimide was discontinued and hydrocortisone was tapered.

raw_record.support_text: The hepatotoxic effects of tacrine occur in nearly half the patients treated with it. Although some patients have had increases in serum ALT as high as 20 times the upper limit of normal, no deaths have been associated with tacrine hepatotoxicity. Tacrine is described as a relatively pure hepatocellular toxin, with ALT increases usually without concomitant increases in alkaline phosphatase or bilirubin, and hepatotoxicity does not seem to be dose related.

raw_record.extra_details: 47% of permanently withdrawn patients were withdrawn due to pronounced ALT increases; 49% of controlled-trial patients had at least one increased ALT, 25% had ALT >3x ULN, and 2% had ALT >20x ULN; no deaths from tacrine hepatotoxicity; raised ALT was delayed with peak incidence at 6-8 weeks of exposure and 90% of increases by week 12; not dose related; age, weight, and concomitant drug/alcohol/nicotine use did not predict risk; ALT increases usually without alkaline phosphatase or bilirubin rises; jaundice indicates severe liver injury and mandates drug withdrawal and supportive therapy; some patients have malaise or nausea/vomiting, many are symptom-free; data from controlled clinical trials (n=634 tacrine, n=342 placebo) and Cognex package insert.

raw_record.support_text: This paper characterizes tacrine-induced liver injury in humans. Of 636 patients developing elevated transaminases during clinical trials, 5 had jaundice; all had ALT >3x ULN, 3 had significant alkaline phosphatase elevation, and 1 significant bilirubin elevation, and 3 patients recovered on drug discontinuation. A Hammel et al. case reported acute hepatitis in a 76-year-old woman after 20 days of tacrine 75 mg/d (jaundice and fever, markedly elevated bilirubin and ALT), with a liver biopsy showing marked centrilobular hepatocyte necrosis and mild inflammatory infiltration, and LFTs normal five days after discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: From NDA clinical-trial data: 636 patients developed elevated transaminases, 5 with jaundice (all ALT >3x ULN, 3 significant alkaline phosphatase elevation, 1 significant bilirubin elevation); 3 recovered on discontinuation. Manufacturer biopsy data for 7 patients with elevated transaminases showed hepatocellular necrosis in 6 and granulomatous hepatitis in 1; an Australian study of 4 patients with asymptomatic liver-enzyme increases found focal necrosis with slight fatty changes (1 with granulomatous hepatitis). Of 56 rechallenged patients in one study, 21.4% discontinued due to recurrence of elevated LFTs, with mean time to ALT elevation of 19 days (faster than initial onset). Liver tests reverted to normal within 5 months. Patient also continuously took antidiabetic drugs and enalapril during the whole period. Authors note propafenone hepatotoxicity is very rare (only three prior published cases) and suggest accumulation of toxic hepatic metabolites and enterohepatic recirculation may account for the injury.

raw_record.support_text: A letter to the editor reports two patients who had received phenelzine (a monoamine oxidase inhibitor for depression) for 4 months at 22.5 mg and 60 mg twice daily, respectively, and who required emergency orthotopic liver transplantation because of fulminant hepatic failure. Phenelzine-induced fulminant hepatic failure was diagnosed after biochemical, serologic, immunologic, hematologic, and histologic studies ruled out other known causes of liver damage. The cases fit the pattern of hydrazine-derivative-induced hepatotoxic injury: delayed toxic effect, no evidence of hypersensitivity-mediated injury, and predominantly hepatocellular rather than cholestatic damage. The paper states the mechanism by which a hydrazine derivative such as phenelzine causes hepatic injury appears to be idiosyncratic, and notes that advanced age, simultaneous enzymatic induction by alcohol or other drugs, and coincident viral infection may play roles, while the relation with the rapid acetylator phenotype remains controversial.
raw_record.extra_details: Two patients treated with phenelzine for 4 months at 22.5 mg and 60 mg twice daily, respectively; both required emergency orthotopic liver transplantation for fulminant hepatic failure (reported as the first two such cases successfully treated by transplant with other causes ruled out). Presented as severe phenelzine-induced hepatitis; pattern matches hydrazine-derivative-induced injury: delayed toxic effect, no hypersensitivity, predominantly hepatocellular (rather than cholestatic) histology. Potential contributing roles of advanced age, enzymatic induction by alcohol/other drugs, and coincident viral infection proposed; possible relation with rapid acetylator phenotype noted as controversial.

raw_record.support_text: A 19-year-old man (case 2) developed jaundice, pruritus, and epigastric discomfort after taking terfenadine 60 mg twice daily for 4 weeks (he had no other medications, herbal remedies, or risk factors for hepatitis). Initial liver tests were AST 232 IU/L, ALT 665 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 146 IU/L, and total bilirubin 185 µmol/L; a liver biopsy showed centrilobular intracellular and intracanalicular cholestasis, mild portal fibrosis, and inflammation with neutrophilic and eosinophilic leucocytes, compatible with drug-induced hepatotoxicity. After terfenadine was stopped, bilirubin rose to a maximum of 909 µmol/L but liver function tests returned to normal within 3 months.

Liver biopsy showed preservation of architecture with centrilobular intra- and intracanalicular cholestasis, mild portal tract fibrosis, and inflammation with neutrophilic and eosinophilic leucocytes. No rechallenge performed in either case due to severity of the initial episode; causality supported by temporal relation, absence of other identifiable causes of hepatitis, and compatible histology. The paper notes the reaction is rare and 'probably idiosyncratic', that a product monograph (Seldane) reported isolated cases of jaundice, cholestatic hepatitis and hepatitis without clear causality, and that only one prior report of possible terfenadine hepatitis (without histology) was found. Recovery within 3 months.

raw_record.support_text: Tacrine, the first cholinesterase inhibitor widely used for Alzheimer's disease, produced hepatotoxicity in clinical trials. The high study attrition rate in the pivotal 30-week trial of tacrine was attributed to hepatotoxicity and cholinergic side effects, and hepatotoxicity, along with frequent cholinergic side effects and a short half-life requiring qid dosing, limited the widespread use of tacrine.
